fields.lead: Working out when and how plate tectonics began, how plates and the deep mantle drive each other, and how faults release stress in both slow and fast slip.

papers.title: Convection plumes in the lower mantle
papers.why: Proposed that hotspots like Hawaii sit above narrow plumes rising from deep in the mantle. Whether plumes exist and where they come from is still argued over, now with seismic imaging.

papers.title: On the relative importance of the driving forces of plate motion
papers.venue: Geophysical Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society
papers.why: Compared plate speeds with plate features and concluded that sinking slabs pull plates more than ridges push them. Slab pull remains the starting point for plate-driving models.

papers.title: Mantle convection and plate tectonics: toward an integrated physical and chemical theory
papers.why: Laid out why mantle convection models struggled to produce plates and what was needed to fix that. Self-consistent plate generation is still a main goal of geodynamic modeling.

papers.title: Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago
papers.why: Used tiny zircon crystals to argue for crust and liquid water within 150 million years of Earth's formation. These zircons are central to the debate over what the early Earth was like.

papers.title: Episodic tremor and slip on the Cascadia subduction zone: the chatter of silent slip
papers.why: Found that slow slip on the Cascadia fault repeats regularly and comes with seismic tremor. Slow earthquakes are now a major research area because they may load faults toward big ones.

papers.title: Evidence from ophiolites, blueschists, and ultrahigh-pressure metamorphic terranes that the modern episode of subduction tectonics began in Neoproterozoic time
papers.why: Argued that modern-style subduction began less than a billion years ago. It sits at one end of the wide debate over when plate tectonics started.

papers.title: Age, spreading rates, and spreading asymmetry of the world's ocean crust
papers.why: Produced a global map of seafloor age and spreading rates. It is a standard input for plate reconstructions, sea-level and mantle models.

papers.title: Structure and dynamics of Earth's lower mantle
papers.why: Reviewed the two large blobs of slow seismic speed at the base of the mantle and what they might be. Their origin and role in plumes is still open.

papers.title: Plate tectonics, damage and inheritance
papers.why: Proposed that weakened zones in the lithosphere build up and persist over time, letting plate tectonics start slowly. It is a leading physical model for how plates first formed.

papers.title: Broad plumes rooted at the base of the Earth's mantle beneath major hotspots
papers.why: Used whole-mantle seismic imaging to find broad plumes beneath major hotspots. It revived the plume hypothesis and linked plumes to the deep mantle blobs.

more.title: Cenozoic tectonics of Asia: effects of a continental collision
more.why: Explained Asia's faults and mountains as the result of India's collision. How continents deform, as blocks or as a continuum, is still debated using this case.

more.title: Mantle geochemistry: the message from oceanic volcanism
more.why: Reviewed how ocean-island lavas show recycled crust in the mantle. It frames how geochemistry is used to trace mantle structure.

more.title: Evidence for deep mantle circulation from global tomography
more.why: Imaged sinking slabs reaching the lower mantle. It largely ended the idea of a mantle split into separate layers.

more.title: Nonvolcanic deep tremor associated with subduction in southwest Japan
more.why: Discovered tremor deep under Japan unlike ordinary earthquakes. Together with Cascadia, it opened the study of slow earthquakes.

more.title: Large igneous provinces generated from the margins of the large low-velocity provinces in the deep mantle
more.why: Found that past large eruptions plot above the edges of the deep mantle blobs. It suggests these structures have been stable for hundreds of millions of years.

more.title: A scaling law for slow earthquakes
more.why: Showed slow earthquakes follow a different size-duration law from ordinary ones. It set up slow slip as a distinct process to explain.

more.title: The 2011 magnitude 9.0 Tohoku-Oki earthquake: mosaicking the megathrust from seconds to centuries
more.why: Showed how unexpectedly large slip occurred near the trench. It changed hazard thinking about which fault segments can host giant earthquakes.

more.title: Archean upper crust transition from mafic to felsic marks the onset of plate tectonics
more.why: Used trace elements to argue continental crust changed composition around three billion years ago. It places the start of plate tectonics far earlier than Stern does.

more.title: Geological archive of the onset of plate tectonics
more.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A
more.why: Reviewed the rock evidence for when plate tectonics began. It is a standard summary of a still-unsettled question.
more.note: Title and author list not checked this pass.

more.title: Moon-forming impactor as a source of Earth's basal mantle anomalies
more.why: Proposed that the deep mantle blobs are remains of the body that hit Earth and formed the Moon. It is a new and contested idea about their origin.

fields.lead: Narrowing how much warming a given amount of carbon dioxide causes, and working out the regional extremes and tipping risks that follow.

papers.title: Thermal equilibrium of the atmosphere with a given distribution of relative humidity
papers.why: Gave the first realistic estimate of warming from doubled carbon dioxide, including water vapor feedback. Its approach and its answer still hold, and it remains the base of climate modeling.

papers.title: Variations in the Earth's orbit: pacemaker of the ice ages
papers.why: Showed that ice ages follow cycles in Earth's orbit. Why the climate responds so strongly to small orbital changes is still debated.

papers.title: Climate and atmospheric history of the past 420,000 years from the Vostok ice core, Antarctica
papers.why: Showed that carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together over four ice-age cycles. Ice-core records remain a key check on climate sensitivity.

papers.title: A new method for diagnosing radiative forcing and climate sensitivity
papers.why: Introduced a simple regression for getting forcing and feedback from model runs. It is now the standard way climate sensitivity is measured in models.

papers.title: Human contribution to the European heatwave of 2003
papers.why: Showed that human influence had at least doubled the risk of the 2003 heatwave. It started event attribution, now done routinely after major disasters.

papers.title: Robust responses of the hydrological cycle to global warming
papers.why: Explained why warming makes wet regions wetter and dry regions drier, while convection slows. These rules of thumb still frame how rainfall change is understood.

papers.title: Tipping elements in the Earth's climate system
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.why: Identified parts of the climate system that could shift abruptly, such as ice sheets and the Amazon. Tipping risk now shapes climate policy and research.

papers.title: Warming caused by cumulative carbon emissions towards the trillionth tonne
papers.why: Showed that peak warming depends mainly on total carbon emitted. Carbon budgets in IPCC reports and net-zero targets rest on this.

papers.title: A reconstruction of regional and global temperature for the past 11,300 years
papers.why: Reconstructed temperature since the last ice age and showed today's warming is unusual. Its disagreement with models, the 'Holocene temperature conundrum', is still being worked on.

papers.title: An assessment of Earth's climate sensitivity using multiple lines of evidence
papers.why: Combined physical, historical and paleoclimate evidence to narrow climate sensitivity to about 2.6-3.9 degrees. It underpinned the IPCC's tighter range.

more.title: Stochastic climate models. Part I. Theory
more.why: Showed that slow climate variability can come from integrating fast weather noise. It underlies how natural variability is separated from forced change.

more.title: High-resolution carbon dioxide concentration record 650,000-800,000 years before present
more.why: Extended the ice-core carbon dioxide record to 800,000 years. It shows today's levels are far outside that range.

more.title: Greenhouse-gas emission targets for limiting global warming to 2 °C
more.why: Turned temperature targets into emissions budgets with probabilities. It shaped how targets like the Paris goals are framed.

more.title: Global warming preceded by increasing carbon dioxide concentrations during the last deglaciation
more.why: Showed global temperature lagged carbon dioxide at the end of the last ice age. It settled a common objection about which came first.

more.title: Overview of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) experimental design and organization
more.why: Set the design of the current round of climate model comparisons. Most climate projections today come from CMIP6 runs.

more.title: Contribution of Antarctica to past and future sea-level rise
more.why: Added ice-cliff collapse to Antarctic models and projected much faster sea-level rise. Whether that process is real is one of the biggest open questions in sea-level projection.

more.title: Energy budget constraints on climate sensitivity in light of inconstant climate feedbacks
more.why: Showed that sensitivity estimated from recent warming is biased low because feedbacks change over time. This 'pattern effect' is a live topic in sensitivity research.

more.title: Attribution of weather and climate events
more.venue: Annual Review of Environment and Resources
more.why: Reviewed how scientists attribute single extreme events to climate change. It is the standard overview of a fast-growing field.

more.title: Causes of higher climate sensitivity in CMIP6 models
more.why: Traced the high sensitivity of many new models to cloud feedbacks. It led to the 'hot model' problem in how projections are used.

more.title: Exceeding 1.5°C global warming could trigger multiple climate tipping points
more.why: Updated tipping-point thresholds and found several may be crossed near 1.5 degrees. It is the current reference for tipping risk.

fields.lead: Tracking how the ocean's circulation, heat uptake, oxygen and carbon chemistry are changing, and whether the Atlantic overturning circulation is heading toward collapse.

papers.title: Thermohaline convection with two stable regimes of flow
papers.why: Showed with a simple model that ocean circulation driven by heat and salt can have two stable states. It is the basis for today's fear that the Atlantic circulation could tip.

papers.title: Abyssal recipes II: energetics of tidal and wind mixing
papers.why: Showed that the deep circulation depends on mixing powered by tides and winds, not just on sinking water. Where that mixing happens is still an active research question.

papers.title: Biogeochemical controls and feedbacks on ocean primary production
papers.why: Reviewed how nutrients and plankton control the ocean's uptake of carbon. It frames how ocean biology affects the carbon cycle.

papers.title: Ocean circulation and climate during the past 120,000 years
papers.why: Linked abrupt past climate shifts to changes in the Atlantic circulation. It is the reference case for what a circulation shutdown could do.

papers.title: The oceanic sink for anthropogenic CO2
papers.why: Measured how much human carbon dioxide the ocean has taken up, about half of fossil emissions. Tracking this sink remains central to carbon budgets.

papers.title: Anthropogenic ocean acidification over the twenty-first century and its impact on calcifying organisms
papers.why: Projected that parts of the ocean will become corrosive to shells this century. It made ocean acidification a major research area.

papers.title: World ocean heat content and thermosteric sea level change (0-2000 m), 1955-2010
papers.why: Showed the ocean has absorbed most of the extra heat from global warming. Ocean heat content is now one of the main measures of climate change.

papers.title: Closing the meridional overturning circulation through Southern Ocean upwelling
papers.why: Showed that winds over the Southern Ocean pull deep water up, closing the global circulation. It shifted attention to the Southern Ocean's role in heat and carbon uptake.

papers.title: Observed fingerprint of a weakening Atlantic Ocean overturning circulation
papers.why: Used a sea-surface temperature pattern to argue the Atlantic circulation has weakened since the mid-twentieth century. The claim is contested, which keeps it at the center of the AMOC debate.

papers.title: A sea change in our view of overturning in the subpolar North Atlantic
papers.why: Reported OSNAP measurements showing most overturning happens east of Greenland, not in the Labrador Sea. It changed where models and monitoring focus.

more.title: Glacial-interglacial CO2 change: the iron hypothesis
more.why: Proposed that iron limits plankton growth and that more dust during ice ages drew down carbon dioxide. Iron limitation is now well established and still drives carbon-removal debates.

more.title: Glacial/interglacial variations in atmospheric carbon dioxide
more.why: Reviewed how the ocean could have stored the carbon missing from the ice-age atmosphere. The question is still not fully settled.

more.title: What is the thermohaline circulation?
more.why: Argued the 'conveyor belt' is a misleading picture because winds and tides do most of the driving. It reshaped how the overturning circulation is described.

more.title: The Argo Program: observing the global ocean with profiling floats
more.why: Described the global network of floats that measure ocean temperature and salinity. Argo data underpin nearly all modern estimates of ocean heat.

more.title: Global observations of nonlinear mesoscale eddies
more.why: Mapped eddies worldwide from satellites and showed they carry heat and nutrients. Representing eddies is a main challenge for climate models.

more.title: Decline in global oceanic oxygen content during the past five decades
more.why: Found the ocean has lost about two percent of its oxygen since 1960. Deoxygenation is now a major concern for marine life.

more.title: Marine heatwaves under global warming
more.why: Showed marine heatwaves have become more frequent and will increase sharply with warming. It started much of the current work on ocean extremes.

more.title: The oceanic sink for anthropogenic CO2 from 1994 to 2007
more.why: Updated the ocean carbon sink and found it kept pace with rising emissions. It is the reference for whether the sink is weakening.

more.title: Multi-faceted particle pumps drive carbon sequestration in the ocean
more.why: Showed several mechanisms besides sinking particles move carbon into the deep ocean. It reshaped estimates of the biological carbon pump.

more.title: Warning of a forthcoming collapse of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation
more.why: Used statistical early-warning signals to predict an AMOC collapse possibly this century. It is widely debated and has driven new work on tipping risk.

fields.lead: Improving weather and climate prediction, now with machine learning, while clouds, aerosols and changes in extremes remain the biggest sources of uncertainty.

papers.title: Deterministic nonperiodic flow
papers.why: Showed that a simple weather model is chaotic, so small errors grow and limit forecasts. It is why forecasting now uses ensembles of runs.

papers.title: Atmospheric teleconnections from the equatorial Pacific
papers.why: Explained El Niño as a feedback between Pacific winds and ocean temperatures. That feedback is still the core of ENSO prediction.

papers.title: Detection of a 40-50 day oscillation in the zonal wind in the tropical Pacific
papers.why: Found a slow, eastward-moving pattern of tropical rainfall and winds. The Madden-Julian Oscillation is a main source of predictability beyond two weeks, and models still struggle with it.

papers.title: The influence of pollution on the shortwave albedo of clouds
papers.why: Showed that pollution particles make clouds brighter by creating more, smaller droplets. Aerosol effects on clouds are still the largest uncertainty in human climate forcing.

papers.title: Nonlinear axially symmetric circulations in a nearly inviscid atmosphere
papers.why: Gave a simple theory for how wide the tropical Hadley circulation is. It frames current work on why the tropics are expanding.

papers.title: The steady linear response of a spherical atmosphere to thermal and orographic forcing
papers.why: Showed how tropical heating sends wave trains around the globe. It explains how El Niño and other tropical events affect weather far away.

papers.title: Increasing destructiveness of tropical cyclones over the past 30 years
papers.why: Linked rising hurricane destructiveness to warmer oceans. It started the ongoing debate over how climate change affects tropical cyclones.

papers.title: The quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction
papers.why: Described how forecasts gained about a day of skill per decade. It is the baseline that machine-learning forecasting is now measured against.

papers.title: Clouds, circulation and climate sensitivity
papers.why: Argued that understanding how clouds interact with circulation is key to narrowing climate sensitivity. It set the agenda for current field campaigns and modeling.

papers.title: Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting
papers.why: Showed a machine-learning model (GraphCast) beating the leading physics-based forecast on most measures. It has pushed forecasting centers to adopt AI models.

more.title: Aerosols, cloud microphysics, and fractional cloudiness
more.why: Proposed that pollution makes clouds last longer by suppressing rain. How strong this effect is remains a main uncertainty in aerosol forcing.

more.title: An energy-balance analysis of deep convective self-aggregation above uniform SST
more.why: Showed that tropical storms can clump together on their own in uniform conditions. Self-aggregation is an active topic for climate sensitivity.

more.title: Expansion of the Hadley cell under global warming
more.why: Showed models expand the tropics as the climate warms. Tropical widening affects where deserts and storm tracks shift.

more.title: Untangling aerosol effects on clouds and precipitation in a buffered system
more.why: Argued clouds partly buffer aerosol effects, so they may be smaller than thought. It shapes how aerosol-cloud interactions are studied.

more.title: Evidence linking Arctic amplification to extreme weather in mid-latitudes
more.why: Proposed that a warming Arctic makes the jet stream wavier and weather more persistent. The claim is contested, which keeps it live.

more.title: Atmospheric circulation as a source of uncertainty in climate change projections
more.why: Argued that changes in circulation, not just temperature, drive regional climate uncertainty. It shaped storyline approaches to regional projections.

more.title: Emergence of healing in the Antarctic ozone layer
more.why: Found the first signs of the Antarctic ozone hole recovering. It shows the Montreal Protocol working and is the baseline for tracking recovery.

more.title: Bounding global aerosol radiative forcing of climate change
more.why: Combined evidence to constrain how much aerosols have cooled the planet. It sets the range used in recent assessments.

more.title: Global increase in major tropical cyclone exceedance probability over the past four decades
more.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
more.why: Found the share of storms reaching major intensity has risen globally since 1979. It is the main observational evidence for stronger tropical cyclones.

more.title: Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning
more.why: Showed a machine-learning ensemble (GenCast) beating the leading physics-based ensemble forecast. It moved AI weather models toward probabilistic forecasting.
more.note: Published online Dec 2024; issue year 2025 assumed.

fields.lead: Dating mass extinctions precisely, working out when animals and major groups arose, and using the fossil record to judge today's biodiversity loss.

papers.title: Punctuated equilibria: the tempo and mode of evolution reconsidered
papers.why: Defended the claim that species mostly stay stable and change in short bursts. How often stasis occurs is still tested with fossil data.

papers.title: Extraterrestrial cause for the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction
papers.why: Found iridium at the extinction boundary and proposed an asteroid impact. The impact is accepted, but its role relative to volcanism is still debated.

papers.title: Mass extinctions in the marine fossil record
papers.why: Identified the 'big five' mass extinctions from fossil counts. This framework is how today's biodiversity loss is compared to the past.

papers.title: Four-winged dinosaurs from China
papers.why: Described Microraptor, a feathered dinosaur with wings on all four limbs. It reshaped ideas about how flight evolved, a question still being worked out.

papers.title: The pectoral fin of Tiktaalik roseae and the origin of the tetrapod limb
papers.why: Showed how a fish fin turned into a limb with joints. It is the main fossil evidence for the move from water to land.

papers.title: Phanerozoic trends in the global diversity of marine invertebrates
papers.why: Corrected the fossil record for sampling and found much less rise in diversity than earlier counts showed. Sampling correction is now standard in the field.

papers.title: The Cambrian conundrum: early divergence and later ecological success in the early history of animals
papers.why: Combined fossils and molecular clocks to show animal lineages split long before they show up as fossils. The gap is still being explained.

papers.title: Has the Earth's sixth mass extinction already arrived?
papers.why: Compared today's extinction rates with the big five using fossil data. It put the 'sixth extinction' on a quantitative footing.

papers.title: Time scales of critical events around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
papers.why: Dated the asteroid impact and the extinction to within tens of thousands of years of each other. High-precision dating is now how competing causes are tested.

papers.title: High-precision timeline for Earth's most severe extinction
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.why: Dated the end-Permian extinction to about 60,000 years. It tied the extinction closely to Siberian volcanism.

more.title: A factor analytic description of the Phanerozoic marine fossil record
more.why: Identified three great evolutionary faunas that dominated the oceans in turn. It is still the standard description of large-scale marine diversity.

more.title: The relative importance of directional change, random walks, and stasis in the evolution of fossil lineages
more.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
more.why: Tested hundreds of fossil sequences and found directional change is rare. It gave a statistical answer to the punctuated equilibrium debate.

more.title: The Red Queen and the Court Jester: species diversity and the role of biotic and abiotic factors through time
more.why: Contrasted competition and environmental change as drivers of diversity. The question of which dominates is still argued.

more.title: The Chicxulub asteroid impact and mass extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
more.why: Pulled together evidence that the impact caused the extinction. It is the main statement of the impact case against volcanism.

more.title: Gradual assembly of avian body plan culminated in rapid rates of evolution across the dinosaur-bird transition
more.why: Showed bird features built up gradually in dinosaurs before a burst of fast evolution. It is the main quantitative picture of how birds arose.

more.title: Uncertainty in the timing of origin of animals and the limits of precision in molecular timescales
more.why: Showed molecular clocks can't pin down the origin of animals precisely. It shapes how fossil and molecular dates are reconciled.

more.title: Early evolution of modern birds structured by global forest collapse at the end-Cretaceous mass extinction
more.why: Argued that forests collapsed after the impact, so only ground-dwelling birds survived. It links extinction selectivity to ecology.

more.title: Ancient steroids establish the Ediacaran fossil Dickinsonia as one of the earliest animals
more.why: Found animal cholesterol in a Dickinsonia fossil, showing it was an animal. It uses molecular fossils to settle a long debate.

more.title: Temperature-dependent hypoxia explains biogeography and severity of end-Permian marine mass extinction
more.why: Showed warming and oxygen loss together explain where and how severely species died out. It links past extinctions to today's ocean changes.

more.title: The spatial structure of Phanerozoic marine animal biodiversity
more.why: Showed that diversity trends depend strongly on the geographic spread of samples. It changed how global diversity curves are built.
